concept.name: Spoofing
concept.definition: Bidding or offering with the intent to cancel the bid or offer before execution, an explicitly prohibited disruptive trading practice under CEA section 4c(a)(5)(C) as added by the Dodd-Frank Act. The spoofer places visible orders it never intends to fill in order to deceive other participants about supply or demand and profit from the induced price movement.
concept.intuition: You wave a huge fake buy order in front of the market so prices tick up, then you sell into the move and yank the fake order before anyone can hit it.
concept.mechanics: A trader enters a large, visible order on one side of the book (the spoof order) while holding or entering a genuine smaller order on the opposite side. The spoof order shifts the quoted imbalance, nudging price toward the genuine order, which executes; the spoof order is then cancelled. Violation requires intent to cancel before execution, as shown by patterns of placement and cancellation.
concept.failure_modes: Because violation turns on intent to cancel, legitimate rapid order modification by market makers can resemble spoofing in surveillance data; regulators distinguish the two using order lifetime, fill ratios, and opposite-side trading patterns, and enforcement has faced acquittals where intent was not proven.
concept.misconceptions: Cancelling orders is not itself illegal — markets depend on cancellation; spoofing requires entering the order with the intent to cancel it before execution in order to mislead others.
concept.example: A trader places a 2,000-lot offer in E-mini S&P futures 2 ticks above market, causing the price to dip into their resting 50-lot bid; once filled, the large offer is cancelled in under a second — the pattern prosecuted in cases like U.S. v. Coscia.

citations.source: CFTC, Antidisruptive Practices Authority (Interpretive Guidance), 78 FR 31890
